summary: Leviticus 17 says that an Israelite who kills a bull, lamb, or goat in or outside the camp must bring it to the Tent as an offering; the explanation then focuses on ending open-field sacrifices to goat idols. It includes resident foreigners in the sacrifice and blood rules and forbids consuming blood because life is in it and God has assigned it to the altar for atonement. Hunted animals receive a separate blood-disposal rule, while eating an animal found dead or torn brings washing and temporary uncleanness.
whyItMatters: The chapter joins exclusive worship with respect for creaturely life: blood is not ordinary food because God designates it for atonement. It also distinguishes deliberate rival sacrifice or blood consumption from the temporary ritual status caused by eating a carcass.

context.author: The text presents this instruction as Yahweh’s word through Moses; authorship and final composition are debated
context.audience: Aaron, his sons, all the children of Israel, and resident foreigners included in the sacrifice and blood rules
context.date: The commands are framed around Israel’s single wilderness tabernacle; the date of final composition is debated
context.setting: Israel’s camp, the open field, and the door of the Tent of Meeting
context.literaryForm: Priestly covenant law governing sacrifice, blood, and carcass impurity

outline.heading: Named livestock brought to the Tent
outline.note: The broad rule about killing bulls, lambs, or goats is followed by its purpose: bringing field sacrifices to the priest and ending goat-idol worship.

outline.heading: One altar rule for Israelite and foreign resident
outline.note: Burnt offerings and sacrifices not brought to the Tent bring the stated sanction of being cut off.

outline.heading: Blood forbidden and given for atonement
outline.note: God sets his face against consuming blood because life is in it and it has an altar function.

outline.heading: A hunter pours out and covers blood
outline.note: The blood of permitted hunted animals or birds is returned to the ground rather than eaten.

outline.heading: A carcass brings temporary uncleanness
outline.note: Native and foreign resident wash after eating an animal that died or was torn, with guilt attached to refusing the cleansing.

keyVerses.text: and hasn’t brought it to the door of the Tent of Meeting to offer it as an offering to Yahweh before Yahweh’s tabernacle: blood shall be imputed to that man. He has shed blood. That man shall be cut off from among his people.
keyVerses.why: Failure to bring the named animal to the Tent is treated as bloodshed with a severe sanction.

keyVerses.text: For the life of the flesh is in the blood. I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls; for it is the blood that makes atonement by reason of the life.
keyVerses.why: The chapter links blood’s altar function to the life it bears.

keyVerses.text: “‘Whatever man there is of the children of Israel, or of the strangers who live as foreigners among them, who takes in hunting any animal or bird that may be eaten, he shall pour out its blood, and cover it with dust.
keyVerses.why: Hunting receives a distinct rule: pour the blood out and cover it with dust.

questions.question: How broad is the opening rule about killing animals?
questions.answer: The opening rule broadly names killing a bull, lamb, or goat inside or outside the camp, requiring the animal to be brought to the Tent as an offering. Its stated purpose then focuses on bringing field sacrifices to God and ending goat-idol worship. Hunting edible animals or birds is treated separately: their blood is poured out and covered with dust.

questions.question: Why are sacrifices centralized at the Tent of Meeting?
questions.answer: The chapter gives its reason: sacrifices formerly offered in the open field are to come to Yahweh’s priest and altar, and Israel is no longer to sacrifice to goat idols. The rule protects exclusive covenant worship in the camp setting described here.

questions.question: What are the “goat idols” mentioned in verse 7?
questions.answer: The WEB uses this label for the recipients of forbidden sacrifices in the open field. The text describes this rival worship through the image of prostitution and commands that it cease. It gives no named figure or detailed description of the idols.

questions.question: Why are resident foreigners included in these rules?
questions.answer: The rules explicitly include foreigners living among Israel when they offer sacrifices, eat, or hunt. Their offerings must come to the Tent, blood is forbidden to them as food, and eating a carcass requires the same washing and waiting as for a native-born person.

questions.question: Why may blood not be eaten?
questions.answer: Verse 11 gives the chapter’s answer: the life of the flesh is in the blood, and God has given blood on the altar to make atonement by reason of that life. Refusing it as food reserves it for the purpose God assigns.

questions.question: Why does verse 4 call this livestock slaughter “bloodshed”?
questions.answer: Verse 4 counts the person who kills the named livestock without bringing it to the Tent as having shed blood and assigns the sanction of being cut off. Verses 5–7 explain that field sacrifices are to come to God’s priest, with blood sprinkled on the altar and fat burned, ending offerings to goat idols. The law therefore makes slaughter of these animals accountable to the sanctuary’s offering requirements.

questions.question: What must a hunter do with an edible animal’s blood?
questions.answer: The hunter pours the blood out and covers it with dust. Unlike a bull, lamb, or goat offered at the Tent, the hunted animal is not turned into a peace offering, but respect for its life-bearing blood still excludes eating it.

questions.question: What does it mean that an offender will be “cut off”?
questions.answer: Being “cut off” is the severe sanction stated for unauthorized sacrifice and consuming blood. In verse 10 God says he will set his face against the person and cut him off; the chapter does not supply a human sentencing procedure or define every form this sanction takes.

questions.question: Why does eating an animal found dead have a different result from deliberately eating blood?
questions.answer: Verses 15-16 give the carcass eater washing, bathing, uncleanness until evening, and then clean status; failure to wash leaves the person bearing iniquity. The preceding blood ban carries the harsher “cut off” language, so the chapter itself distinguishes the cases.

glossary.def: A sacrifice brought to Yahweh at the Tent, with its blood and fat handled by the priest.
The altar work for which God says life-bearing blood has been given.
A severe covenant sanction whose exact mechanism is not specified in this chapter.

reviewer: Codex editorial agents; independent chapter review

before.text: The annual atonement rite has used blood to cleanse sacred spaces and a live goat to carry confessed sins away. Blood’s altar use is now explained alongside rules for slaughter, sacrifice, and food.

here.text: The chapter brings cattle, sheep, and goat slaughter into the Tent’s offering system, forbids rival sacrifice and blood consumption, and distinguishes hunted animals and carcass impurity.

after.text: The next speech turns to sexual and kinship boundaries, prohibits giving children to Molech, and warns that prohibited practices defile the people and the land.
